\subsection*{Setup: the committer machines}

Nineteen machines, each 64 cores and \SI{156}{\gibi\byte}, running three signature verifiers, one
coordinator, one sidecar, one load generator, six validator--committers, twelve YugabyteDB tablet
servers and three YugabyteDB masters. The six validator--committers and the three masters sit on nine
of the twelve database machines, and no machine runs both a validator--committer and a master.

Storage is two \SI{969}{\gibi\byte} XFS volumes per machine, \texttt{noatime}, mounted \texttt{/data1}
and \texttt{/data2}. Each database node passes YugabyteDB both volumes as separate data directories
(\texttt{-{}-fs\_data\_dirs}, one path per volume) rather than a stripe. The sidecar's
ledger uses \texttt{/data1} alone.

Transactions carry two read--write operations over \SI{32}{\byte} keys, \SI{262}{\byte} serialized, in
\num{10000}-transaction blocks, and each transaction slot takes a fresh key, so there are no
read--write conflicts. Signatures are ECDSA P-256. Blocks come from the load generator's embedded mock
ordering service, which cuts and signs them itself and serves them to the sidecar over the Atomic
Broadcast API, so no ordering service is in the path.

A measured point is the highest offered rate that arrived in full, committed within \SI{2}{\percent},
kept p99 under \SI{1}{\second} and held a flat in-flight count, confirmed by a \SI{300}{\second} hold
on a fresh deployment.

\subsection*{Why this setup}

\textbf{The shape is not the paper's.} The published committer deployment is nine
validator--committers on nine database nodes, dual 48-core servers with \SI{64}{\giga\byte}. What
follows therefore compares deployments, not matched hardware.

\textbf{Both volumes, not a stripe}, so YugabyteDB sees the disk boundary and places data across it
itself. This also has to be stated because it is what a wipe must cover: the data directories are
siblings of the deployment directory, not children, so clearing the deployment directory leaves the
database intact --- which silently invalidated every earlier bring-up of the arm in Part~II.

\textbf{ECDSA rather than Ed25519}, so the two arms differ only in whether an ordering service is
present. This was Ed25519 until the generator stopped being the constraint: \texttt{crypto/ecdsa}
signs hedged, building an HMAC-SHA-512 DRBG per signature, which a CPU profile at \num{193000} tps put
at \SI{8.11}{\percent} of process CPU against \SI{8.80}{\percent} for the elliptic-curve multiplication
it feeds --- nonce setup costing more than the work it exists to serve. Deriving the nonce directly is
worth \num{2.06}$\times$ at 32 cores, about \num{709000} signatures a second, above the ceilings below.
Entropy was never the mechanism (\texttt{GetRandom} was \SI{0.54}{\percent}), and two earlier
explanations --- \texttt{getrandom} contention, then unspecific allocation --- were both wrong.

\textbf{A conflict-free workload} measures the pipeline's ceiling rather than its conflict behaviour,
at the cost of a state database and a ledger that grow with every transaction. Conflicts are then
introduced deliberately as their own variable.

\textbf{Queue flatness is part of the definition} because a rate can be committed in full out of a
growing queue, which reports the queue's drain time as latency.

\subsection*{Throughput and tail latency}

Throughput falls with transaction size (Fig.~\ref{fig:panels}), \num{604545} tps at one read--write
operation to \num{274364} at four: \SI{55}{\percent} against the published \SI{41}{\percent}. The
mechanism is not the published one, which is lock contention in the coordinator's dependency graph.
Here both lock-wait histograms have a count rate of exactly zero, and the graph's cost is per key
instead --- about \SI{420}{\nano\second} each, flat from one key per transaction to eight.

Invalid signatures are close to free but never profitable: \num{558364} tps with none, then
\num{517455}, \num{519455} and \num{518727} at \SI{10}{\percent}, \SI{20}{\percent} and
\SI{30}{\percent} --- flat within \SI{0.4}{\percent}, not the published \SI{10}{\percent} \emph{gain}.
Driven instead at one common \num{559872} tps, all three deliver it while the tail grows with the
invalid share (\SI{1.1}{}, \SI{5.0}{} and \SI{7.5}{\second}): rejection is cheap in throughput and
expensive in latency.

Double spends do not reproduce, and a deployment setting is why. At the 120-way tablet pre-split this
cluster uses, \SI{0}{\percent} holds \num{518000} tps and \emph{no} rate qualifies at \SI{5}{\percent}
or above --- about \num{20000} tps at tens of seconds with every machine under \SI{10}{\percent} CPU,
so neither capacity nor a queue. At the default split the same shapes hold: \num{41273}, \num{30000}
and \num{40909} tps at \SI{10}{\percent}, \SI{20}{\percent} and \SI{30}{\percent} with
\SIrange{334}{533}{\milli\second} p99, flat rather than declining --- while costing the conflict-free
case \num{1.8}$\times$ (\num{518000} against \num{294893}). The split is therefore a
workload-dependent trade, not a tuning win. Narrowing the graph's chunk width refuted multi-key
batching as the mechanism, leaving why 120 tablets collapse unresolved.

\subsection*{What latency costs at a given throughput}

At \num{10000}-transaction blocks the median has a floor near \SI{125}{\milli\second} that does not
fall with the rate, since nothing in a block moves until the block is cut (Fig.~\ref{fig:curve}). At
500 transactions a block the floor is \SI{40}{\milli\second}, and \num{380100} tps holds at
\SI{125}{\milli\second} median and \SI{208}{\milli\second} p99 --- the median large blocks give at
\num{10000} tps, at thirty-eight times the rate. The top of that curve measures the generator, whose
block preparation caps it near 850 blocks a second (\num{425000} tps at this size; \num{450000}
offered delivered \num{432309}), so the committer's own ceiling at 500 transactions is not yet known.

\section*{Part II --- End to end, with a real ordering service}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures-e2e/latency-throughput.pdf}
  \caption{Latency against throughput end to end, with a real ordering service in the path, by shard
  count and batcher storage layout. Marks as in Fig.~\ref{fig:curve}. The axis is clipped at
  \SI{1000}{\milli\second} rather than \SI{400}{\milli\second}, because here the batchers cut the
  blocks with a \SI{500}{\milli\second} \texttt{BatchCreationTimeout} and the median floor sits above
  \SI{400}{\milli\second}. The dotted line is the published ordering-alone figure for this topology.}
  \label{fig:e2e}
\end{figure*}

The second arm puts a real Arma ordering service in the path. The committer tier is
\textbf{unchanged from Part~I} --- the same nineteen machines, the same components, the same tuning ---
so a difference between the two arms is attributable to ordering.

\subsection*{Setup: the ordering machines}

Twenty further machines, each 32 cores and \SI{78}{\gibi\byte}, holding four parties of a router, a
consenter, an assembler and one batcher per shard. Routers, consenters and assemblers take a machine
each, twelve in all; the batchers share the remaining eight. Two configurations are compared:

\begin{itemize}\itemsep2pt
  \item \textbf{Four shards.} Sixteen batchers, two to a machine, each with a volume to itself
  (\texttt{/data1} and \texttt{/data2}).
  \item \textbf{Eight shards.} Thirty-two batchers, four to a machine, two sharing each volume.
\end{itemize}

Storage is two \SI{485}{\gibi\byte} XFS volumes per machine, mounted as on the committer machines.
Routers, consenters and assemblers write to \texttt{/data1}; the batchers are distributed across both
volumes as above.

Blocks are cut by the batchers, so the block-size knob on this arm is the shared configuration's
\texttt{Batching.BatchSize.MaxMessageCount}, not a load-generator setting, and
\texttt{BatchCreationTimeout} is \SI{500}{\milli\second}. Signatures are ECDSA P-256, as in Part~I,
and here the policy derives from a real MSP identity so no other scheme is available. The namespace is
created by \texttt{fxconfig} before load is applied, because the transaction that creates it endorses
against an MSP rule that the load generator has no material for.

\subsection*{Why this setup}

\textbf{Two batchers to a machine} is measured rather than assumed. At two shards the service capped
near \num{158000} tps \emph{per shard} whatever the batch size or decision interval, while batcher
processes sat at \SIrange{15}{20}{\percent} of a 32-core machine --- so the constraint is per shard and
the spare capacity for a second was already on the box.

\textbf{Both shard counts are measured} because that reading predicts more shards buy throughput, and
the two configurations separate the two things a shard needs: a core budget and a disk. Four shards
give each co-located batcher its own volume; eight give twice the shards but make two share one.

\textbf{These machines are half a committer machine} --- half the cores, half the memory and, per
Table~\ref{tab:disk}, half the disk bandwidth --- so a ceiling measured on this arm belongs to these
machines before it belongs to ordering.

\subsection*{Shard count and storage}

Both configurations sustain the same throughput and hit the same knee: \num{499091} tps at four
shards against \num{500000} at eight, \SI{0.2}{\percent} apart, and neither sustains \num{550000}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:e2e}). Four shards is the better configuration on every other axis --- p99 lower by
\SIrange{100}{250}{\milli\second} at every matched rate from \num{100000} tps up
(\SI{658}{\milli\second} against \SI{754}{\milli\second} at the knee), fewer processes, and a volume
per batcher rather than two sharing one.

Doubling the shards buys nothing because ordering is not what limits this arm. Through \num{400000}
tps the busiest machine is a router; from \num{450000} on it is a validator--committer at
\SIrange{78}{82}{\percent}, on both configurations and at low fill as well as high. Extra shards add
capacity to the tier that is not binding.

They also cost latency, for a reason the block size makes plain. At a given total rate each of eight
shards sees half the per-shard rate that four do, so batches take twice as long to reach
\num{10000} transactions and the \SI{500}{\milli\second} \texttt{BatchCreationTimeout} cuts them early
over twice as wide a range of rates. The eight-shard curve shows exactly that shape: p99 rises to
\SI{793}{\milli\second} at \num{150000} tps, then falls monotonically ---
\SI{687}{}, \SI{614}{}, \SI{591}{\milli\second} --- as the rate grows enough to fill a batch before the
timer fires.

\subsection*{Is the knee the rate, or a full database?}

It is the rate. This needed testing rather than asserting, because each ladder climbs on one
deployment, so offered rate and table fill rise together: over the eight-shard ladder the database
grew from \num{9.4} million rows to \num{1.31} billion, free disk fell from \SI{513}{\giga\byte} to
\SI{62}{\giga\byte}, and database commit latency went from \SI{18}{\milli\second} to
\SI{232}{\milli\second}. On that evidence alone a knee at \num{500000} tps is as consistent with a
full table as with the rate.

The two ladders settle it between them, because they reached the same rungs at very different fill.
At \num{550000} tps four shards failed with \num{843} million rows committed, while eight shards
failed with \num{1104} million --- the emptier database by \SI{24}{\percent}, and it failed too. Had
fill been the cause, the emptier one would have passed. What fill does change is how much gets
delivered at a failing rate: \num{532909} tps at the lower fill against \num{497603} at the higher.
So the ceiling is a rate between \num{500000} and \num{533000} tps, and fill moves the delivered
figure a few percent within it rather than creating the limit.

\subsection*{Latency against throughput, ordering included}

End to end, ordering included, this deployment sustains \num{499091} tps at
\SI{658}{\milli\second} p99, with every offered rate up to that arriving in full and no aborted
transactions at any rung. Two comparisons place it. The published work has no end-to-end figure, but
its ordering service alone reaches \num{430000} tps at four parties and four shards --- so the
complete pipeline here exceeds the published figure for one part of it. And the same committer without
an ordering service reaches \num{604545} tps, so real ordering costs about \SI{17}{\percent} of the
committer's own ceiling rather than an order of magnitude.

\textbf{TODO --- running.} The \num{500}-transaction batch ladder, which the reasoning above predicts
should remove most of the low-rate latency penalty: a batch a twentieth the size fills twenty times
sooner, so the \SI{500}{\milli\second} timer should stop being the binding constraint at low rates.

\subsection*{Transaction size}

\textbf{TODO --- queued.} One configuration held fixed, varying only transaction size across
\SIlist{300;512;1024;2048;4096}{\byte}. The published size sweep is a two-shard measurement falling
\num{413000} to \num{27000} tps over that range, each point within \SI{10}{\percent} of
\SI{120}{\mega\byte\per\second} --- so past \SI{300}{\byte} it is bandwidth-bound and the rate is
simply bytes per second over size. Its shape is the comparable part, not its absolute values, since
this arm runs four or eight shards.

\section*{Storage characterisation}

Table~\ref{tab:disk} gives \texttt{fio} 3.35 in the four patterns this deployment produces. The volumes
are \texttt{virtio} devices reporting neither a model nor a meaningful rotational flag, so the backing
media cannot be identified from inside the guest and is characterised by measurement instead.

Two things follow. Ordering machines have half the disk bandwidth as well as half the cores, at almost
exactly a factor of two on every bandwidth row, at round figures, repeating to four significant
figures across machines and volumes --- these are provisioned caps, not device characteristics, so a
ceiling on that arm must be read against the cap before it is attributed to ordering. And durability
is the expensive direction: making one \SI{4}{\kibi\byte} record durable with an \texttt{O\_DSYNC}
write costs about \SI{400}{\micro\second}, capping any per-record design near \num{2400} operations a
second, three orders of magnitude below the rates measured here. The ledger survives that only by
batching --- it appends a whole block and syncs every hundredth. Syncing alone is cheap by comparison,
an \texttt{fdatasync} after a buffered write returning in about \SI{0.08}{\milli\second}: it is the
write, not the barrier, that costs.

\section*{Threats to validity}

The load generator is the instrument and twice became the limit: ECDSA signing, resolved by deriving
the nonce directly, and block preparation, which caps the small-block curve in Fig.~\ref{fig:curve}. A
knee is resolved to the search's \SI{8}{\percent} step, so it is a lower bound, drawn one-sided in
Fig.~\ref{fig:panels}. The baseline drifts \SI{10}{\percent} between days, so only same-day
comparisons are used.

The Part~I figures were measured with Ed25519 signatures, before the ECDSA path was fast enough to
carry them. The setup now specifies ECDSA for both arms; those figures will be re-measured under it,
and until they are, Part~I and Part~II differ in signature scheme as well as in ordering.

One limit is stated in advance of the end-to-end data rather than after it. That arm measures a ladder
on a single deployment, so rate and table fill rise together and the ladder cannot separate them: if
its curve bends upward at the top, that is as consistent with a fuller database as with the offered
rate. On the committer arm the question was settled by holding the rate fixed while fill grew through
one \SI{375}{\second} window, where commit latency stayed flat ---
\SIrange{142.2}{143.0}{\milli\second} across \SI{68}{\percent} fill growth --- but that test belongs to
that arm and does not transfer. Until it is repeated here, an upward bend in the end-to-end curve is
not attributable to rate. Each rung records the fill it ran against, so the question stays auditable
rather than lost.
